questions.q: How old is Valli, and what is the one thing she does every day that shows her fascination with the bus?
questions.a: Valli is eight years old. Every day she stands at her front doorway and watches the bus that travels between her village and the nearest town. A wrong answer (e.g., "she plays near the bus stop" or "she asks her mother about the bus") reveals the student has not grasped the specific textual detail that her curiosity begins with silent, consistent observation from a fixed spot — her doorway — which the author uses to establish her as a watcher before she becomes a doer.

questions.q: In your own words, explain why the bus journey fascinates Valli more than anything else in her daily life.
questions.a: The bus represents the unknown world beyond her village — new sights, new people, movement, and adulthood. It is the only link between her small world and the larger town. A wrong answer focusing only on "the bus is colourful" or "she likes vehicles" misses the symbolic weight: the bus is a threshold. Students who give this answer confuse surface attraction with the deeper literary function — the bus as a metaphor for transition and possibility.

questions.q: Read this new sentence: "Arjun, ten, watches the metro train pass his apartment every morning, noting the stations announced, the crowd at each stop, and the fare displayed on the screen." Identify two ways Arjun's behaviour mirrors Valli's curiosity in the story.
questions.a: 1) Both observe a regular transport vehicle from a fixed daily spot (doorway/apartment). 2) Both move beyond watching to actively noting specific details (stations/fare/crowd vs. Valli calculating fare, journey time, listening to conversations). A wrong answer listing only "they both watch" fails to apply the concept of *systematic information-gathering* — the hallmark of Valli's curiosity that distinguishes it from passive looking.

questions.q: Compare Valli's curiosity in the opening pages with Suraj's curiosity in "The Tunnel" (Class 6). How does each author use the child's curiosity to reveal character? Give one similarity and one difference.
questions.a: Similarity: Both children are drawn to a mysterious, slightly dangerous "grown-up" space (bus/tunnel) that represents the unknown. Difference: Suraj's curiosity is impulsive and physical — he enters the tunnel immediately. Valli's curiosity is patient and intellectual — she watches, listens, calculates, and plans for months before acting. A wrong answer that says "both are brave" misses the analytical task: the question asks *how the author uses curiosity to reveal character*, not just what the characters do.

questions.q: "Valli's curiosity is a sign of intelligence, not just childish wonder." Defend or challenge this statement using two pieces of evidence from the text.
questions.a: Defend. Evidence 1: She "calculated and recalculated" the fare (thirty paise) and journey time (forty-five minutes) — showing mathematical reasoning. Evidence 2: She "listened carefully to conversations" between passengers and "asked discreet questions" — showing strategic information-gathering. A wrong answer that only cites "she really wanted to go" or "she was excited" reveals the student cannot distinguish between emotional desire and cognitive processing — a critical board exam distinction.

questions.q: Write a 50-word diary entry from Valli's perspective on a day she watched the bus but learned a new detail (e.g., the conductor's name, a new stop). Use first person and show her curiosity at work.
questions.a: A strong entry includes: (1) sensory detail (sound of bus, dust), (2) a specific new fact learned, (3) internal calculation or planning, (4) emotional tone of anticipation. Example: "The bus coughed past today, red and loud. I heard the conductor call out 'Kovalam — ten minutes!' New stop! That means the route extends. Thirty paise still? Must ask tomorrow. My heart beats fast." A poor entry writes only feelings ("I so happy") without the *active curiosity* — noting, questioning, calculating — that defines Valli.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: This node ______ Valli, an eight-year-old girl whose intense curiosity about the bus that passes her village daily becomes the driving force of the narrative.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are ______ years old and every day at the same time, a bright colorful bus roars past your house — where does it go?
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can identify at least three specific textual details that demonstrate Valli's curiosity, explain how the author uses these details to build her character, and connect her curiosity to the broader theme of a child's desire to explore the unknown.
